kid.question: Which group does Micah say judges for reward?

options.text: The priests of the sanctuary
The heads of the city
The prophets of the people
The merchants of the marketplace

kid.explanation: Micah says the heads judge for reward, alongside priests teaching for hire and prophets divining for money.

kid.question: What will Jerusalem become in Micah's warning?

options.text: A center of trade
A garden of olives
A camp of refugees
A heap of ruins

kid.explanation: Because of the leaders' conduct, Zion will be plowed and Jerusalem will become heaps.

kid.question: Why do many nations want to go to the Lord's house?

options.text: To learn His ways
To offer their crowns
To build new walls
To divide their lands

kid.explanation: The nations say God will teach them His ways and they will walk in His paths.

kid.question: What will the nations make from their swords?

options.text: Plowshares
Pruninghooks
Temple lamps
Shepherds' staffs

kid.explanation: Swords become plowshares, while spears become pruninghooks, as the nations cease learning war.

kid.question: Where will each person sit without fear?

options.text: Beside a well and city gate
Inside a tower and fortress
Under a vine and fig tree
Near an altar and temple court

kid.explanation: The promise pictures each person under a vine and fig tree with none making them afraid.

kid.question: Whom does the Lord promise to gather?

options.text: Those serving kings and governors
Those driven away and afflicted
Those selling grain and livestock
Those guarding gates and towers

kid.explanation: The Lord gathers the lame, driven out, and afflicted, making a remnant and a strong nation.

kid.question: Where will Zion go and then be rescued?

options.text: Damascus
Samaria
Nineveh
Babylon

kid.explanation: Zion will go to Babylon, and there the Lord will deliver and redeem her from enemies.

kid.question: From which little place will Israel's ruler come?

options.text: Moresheth-gath
Kiriath-jearim
Bethlehem Ephratah
Jabesh-gilead

kid.explanation: Micah names little Bethlehem Ephratah as the place from which the ruler in Israel will come.

kid.question: What does the Lord say He will remove from His people in Micah 5:10?

options.text: Sheep and shepherds
Horses and chariots
Grapes and vineyards
Silver and merchants

kid.explanation: The Lord says He will cut off their horses and destroy their chariots.

kid.question: Who went ahead of Israel when God rescued them from Egypt?

options.text: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Joshua, Caleb, and Eleazar
David, Solomon, and Nathan

kid.explanation: The Lord recalls redeeming Israel from bondage and sending Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before them.

high-school.question: What claim do the corrupt leaders make alongside their paid judgments and religious service?

options.text: The king has approved them, so foreign armies must obey them
Their ancestors were faithful, so their present debts have been canceled
Their offerings are plentiful, so returning exiles must pay them tribute
The Lord is among them, so disaster cannot come upon them

high-school.explanation: Leaders profit from judging, teaching, and divining yet claim the Lord's presence guarantees safety; destruction is announced instead.

high-school.question: How does the vision of Zion in Micah 4 answer the ruin announced in Micah 3?

options.text: A devastated mountain is later abandoned for a sanctuary in Babylon
A devastated mountain is later exalted as a place of instruction
A devastated mountain is later divided among competing foreign kings
A devastated mountain is later fortified against approaching pilgrims

high-school.explanation: The ruined temple mountain is followed by a last-days vision of the Lord's house exalted and nations coming to learn.

high-school.question: What change joins the making of farming tools in Micah 4?

options.text: Nations stop fighting and learning war
Nations train farmers to defend their borders
Nations send soldiers to collect harvest tribute
Nations exchange weapons for royal building supplies

high-school.explanation: The weapon transformations accompany the promise that nation will not fight nation or learn war anymore.

high-school.question: How are those cast off transformed in the gathering promise?

options.text: The outcasts become hired soldiers under Assyria's king
The outcasts become temple servants under foreign priests
The outcasts become a strong nation under the Lord
The outcasts become trading partners under Babylon's governors

high-school.explanation: The Lord makes the lame a remnant and those cast far off a strong nation, reigning over them in Zion.

high-school.question: What surprising location becomes the place of Zion's redemption?

options.text: The Egypt from which she once escaped
The Assyria from which an army approaches
The Babylon to which she is sent
The wilderness through which she first traveled

high-school.explanation: Zion goes out of the city to Babylon, and the text twice says that deliverance will happen there.

high-school.question: What do the hostile nations fail to understand about their gathering?

options.text: The Lord gathers them like sheaves for threshing
The Lord gathers them as pilgrims to receive instruction
The Lord gathers them as workers to rebuild the city
The Lord gathers them as allies to escort returning captives

high-school.explanation: Nations gather to see Zion defiled, unaware that the Lord gathers them as sheaves and calls Zion to thresh.

high-school.question: What contrast marks the ruler's origin in Micah 5:2?

options.text: A royal birthplace accompanies a reign limited to one generation
A small birthplace accompanies goings forth from everlasting
A foreign birthplace accompanies descent from the house of Aaron
A fortified birthplace accompanies authority granted by Assyria

high-school.explanation: Little Bethlehem Ephratah is named alongside the ruler's goings forth from of old, from everlasting.

high-school.question: Which two images portray Jacob's remnant among other peoples?

options.text: Rain on mountains and a dove among branches
Fire in a forest and a lamb among wolves
Seed in a field and an eagle above cliffs
Dew on grass and a lion among flocks

high-school.explanation: The remnant is compared first to dew and showers, then to a lion among beasts and sheep.

high-school.question: What kinds of reliance are targeted together in Micah 5:10-14?

options.text: Foreign trade, family inheritance, and seasonal crop storage
Military resources, divination, and handmade objects of worship
Temple singers, public teaching, and annual festival offerings
Royal marriage, written treaties, and tribal boundary markers

high-school.explanation: Horses, chariots, strongholds, witchcrafts, soothsayers, and images are named for removal.

high-school.question: How does the Lord begin His case against Israel in Micah 6?

options.text: He calculates tribute and asks when they will repay it
He lists lost battles and asks who commanded the armies
He recalls rescue and asks how He has wearied them
He measures the temple and asks who will enlarge it

high-school.explanation: The controversy asks what the Lord has done to weary Israel, then recalls redemption from Egypt and His earlier righteous acts.

expert.question: What rationale does the announcement of Zion's destruction assign?

options.text: The city's small territory makes its defenses impossible to maintain
The priests' departure leaves the sanctuary without appointed service
The leaders' corruption makes the city vulnerable to judgment
The people's exile prevents cultivation of the surrounding vineyards

expert.explanation: After bloodshed and paid judgments, teaching, and divination, Micah says Zion will be plowed 'for your sake.'

expert.question: How does the direction of instruction in Micah 4:1-2 develop the mountain image?

options.text: Priests ascend to sacrifice, while tribute goes forth from Zion
Peoples ascend to learn, while law goes forth from Zion
Rulers ascend to negotiate, while soldiers go forth from Zion
Exiles ascend to settle, while merchants go forth from Zion

expert.explanation: Nations flow to the exalted house for God's teaching; law and the Lord's word proceed from Zion and Jerusalem.

expert.question: What precedes the disarmament of strong nations in the peace vision?

options.text: The nations' election of a shared earthly ruler
The Lord's judgment and rebuke among peoples
The people's construction of walls around Zion
The priests' distribution of tools to the farmers

expert.explanation: The Lord judges among many peoples and rebukes strong nations before the text describes weapons becoming agricultural tools.

expert.question: How does the statement about walking in the Lord's name relate to the nations?

options.text: It commands temporary withdrawal while others abandon their gods' names
It appoints Israel to rename the gods worshipped among neighboring peoples
It promises Israel a new name after others return their inherited lands
It declares enduring loyalty beside others walking in their gods' names

expert.explanation: After mentioning each people's walk in its god's name, the speakers commit to walking in the Lord's name forever.

expert.question: How does the childbirth image frame Zion's departure to Babylon?

options.text: Severe pain accompanies departure that leads to promised redemption
Severe pain ends the dynasty before a replacement ruler is named
Sudden joy accompanies departure that prevents the announced captivity
Sudden joy rewards the city before an enemy siege can begin

expert.explanation: Zion's travail introduces leaving the city and going to Babylon, where the Lord promises to redeem her.

expert.question: What reverses the hostile nations' intention toward Zion?

options.text: Those seeking her tribute become priests within her restored sanctuary
Those seeking her captives become escorts for her returning rulers
Those seeking her defilement become sheaves for her threshing
Those seeking her fields become workers within her renewed vineyards

expert.explanation: The nations' intention to see Zion defiled is overturned by the Lord's gathering them for Zion to thresh and consecrate their gain.

expert.question: How does the description of the ruler in Micah 5:4 connect authority with security?

options.text: He feeds in the Lord's strength, and his people abide
He rules by Assyria's commission, and his soldiers collect tribute
He reigns through the priests' counsel, and his captives return
He leads by the nobles' consent, and his merchants prosper

expert.explanation: The ruler stands and feeds in the Lord's strength and name; the people abide as his greatness reaches earth's ends.

expert.question: Which pairing best accounts for both the dew and lion images of the remnant?

options.text: Quiet withdrawal and permanent disappearance
Dependence on farmers and obedience to shepherds
Royal prosperity and service at the sanctuary
Refreshing presence and overpowering force

expert.explanation: Dew and showers evoke a different effect from the lion trampling flocks; the passage gives the remnant both images.

expert.question: What legal setting is created by the summons in Micah 6:1-3?

options.text: Mountains mark the territory assigned to the returning tribes
Mountains shelter the witnesses fleeing from Jerusalem's rulers
Mountains hear the Lord's controversy with His people
Mountains supply the stones required for a replacement altar

expert.explanation: The mountains and earth's foundations are called to hear the Lord's controversy and His appeal for Israel to testify.

expert.question: What progression shapes the proposed gifts in Micah 6:6-7?

options.text: Calves give way to public fasting and finally a pilgrimage
Calves escalate to vast offerings and finally one's firstborn
Rams decrease to smaller offerings and finally a confession
Rams give way to rebuilt altars and finally a restored priesthood

expert.explanation: The questions move from year-old calves to thousands of rams, rivers of oil, and a firstborn; the slice stops before verse 8's answer.
